instructions.task: A persuader is chatting with a persuadee to get them to donate to the charity Save the Children. Classify the persuasion strategy or dialogue act of the 'Persuader message to tag' (the last message). Use the earlier dialogue only as context.
rules: Label only the message to tag, not earlier turns.
If the message does several things, pick its main function.
Facts about the charity itself are credibility-appeal; facts about children's suffering are emotion-appeal; arguments that giving makes a difference are logical-appeal.

criteria.greeting: Opening pleasantries: 'hello', 'hi there', 'how are you today?', 'I'm good, how are you?'. Includes the persuader's reply to a how-are-you question: 'Very well thanks.', 'I am doing well, thank you.', 'Doing alright..'.
criteria.closing: Goodbyes and closing wishes at the end of the chat: 'have a great night!', 'I hope you enjoy the rest of your day', 'take care'.
criteria.thank: Thanks the persuadee: 'thank you', 'thanks so much for your donation'.
criteria.praise-user: Explicitly compliments the persuadee as a person: 'you are so kind', 'you're awesome', 'you are a good person', 'people like you make the world better', 'I see I got a really kind person to talk to'. Also praise addressed to the persuadee for their willingness or generosity: 'it is wonderful that you are willing to donate!', 'you're so generous'. (A bare 'That's awesome!' without 'you' is acknowledgement.)
criteria.acknowledgement: A brief, formulaic reaction to the persuadee's last message showing agreement, understanding or a positive reception, adding no content of its own: 'I agree', 'I understand', 'Absolutely', 'That's great to hear', 'That's awesome!', 'Great!', 'Me too', 'I know what you mean'.
criteria.filler: A flat filler with no real content: 'Ok...', 'Fine...', 'yeah..', 'yes, indeed.', 'Indeed.', 'Yes.' as a bare token.
criteria.comment-on-partner: The persuader responds to what the persuadee said with a comment, opinion or answer of their own, rather than a formulaic acknowledgement: 'That's a good idea actually, that way you know your efforts are helping', 'We could all do better, I suppose', 'I do..', 'Yes, they are.', 'Not everyone has it so it's good that you appreciate it'.
criteria.answer-about-self: The persuader answers the persuadee's question about the persuader's own habits or knowledge: 'No, I don't donate', 'Yes, I'm familiar with them', 'I have.' (Replies to 'how are you?' are greeting, not this.)
criteria.confirm-amount: Confirms or repeats back the amount the persuadee chose: 'just to be sure, you want to donate $1?', 'so 20 cents then?'.
criteria.misc-other: Talk about other charities, arguing with or insulting the persuadee, remarks about the HIT/survey/task itself (e.g. 'we need 10 chats to complete this hit', doubts whether money is really deducted), asking for more, non-English text, correcting a typo, a lone URL fix. Also remarks about the conversation itself, e.g. 'let me give you some details so we can finish out this conversation'. Also clarifying questions with no persuasive content ('Which would you prefer?') and unfinished fragments ('Just think.').
criteria.off-task: Chit-chat unrelated to charity or donation: the persuader's or persuadee's hometown, weather, hobbies, work, e.g. 'North Carolina is nice, I have been there once'.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows or has heard of Save the Children: 'Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with the organization?'.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee's opinions, habits or experience about donating or charity, or whether they care about this cause: 'do you donate to charities?', 'have you ever donated to them?', 'is this something you care about?', 'Did you know 5.6 million children die every year...?' asked as a question.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's personal life: 'do you have children?', 'where are you from?', 'tell me about your life'.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asks or urges the persuadee to donate or help, without naming an amount, including hypothetical asks: 'would you like to donate some of your payment to Save the Children?', 'are you willing to donate?', 'if you could do something to help these children, would you?', 'we should donate to them!'.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks how much the persuadee wants to donate: 'how much would you like to give?', 'what amount are you comfortable donating?'.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Asks for a small amount or says even a little helps: 'every little bit helps', 'even $0.50 would help', 'any amount is welcome', 'just a few cents would make a difference'.
criteria.donation-information: Procedural information about how the donation in this task works: it comes out of the task payment, any amount from $0 to $2, the research team collects and sends it, the donation can be made right now. Also practical details of other ways to give or help: no maximum when giving outside the task, tax deductions, payment methods, volunteering options. (Just pointing to the charity website to learn more is credibility-appeal.)
criteria.credibility-appeal: Describes or praises Save the Children: what it is and does, its programs, history, founder, global reach, ratings, trustworthiness, share of funds going to programs, its website; also answers to 'what do they do?' and suffering facts tied to what the charity is doing about them.
criteria.emotion-appeal: Evokes feelings about the children: statistics or vivid descriptions of children dying, starving, killed in war; 'imagine your own child...'; stories about a particular helped child; expressions of sadness or guilt about the children's plight.
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasoning for why one should donate: donations make a real difference, the charity can only help when people donate, moral reasoning such as 'children are the future' or 'everyone deserves a chance', comparing the small cost to the large benefit.
criteria.personal-story: The persuader recounts something they personally experienced or witnessed (first person, past events), to support the cause: 'I worked in Africa and saw the difference a few dollars make', 'I have been to very poor countries and saw how much a little donation helps', 'when I was a kid my family needed help'.
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader states their own donation, intention or habit of giving, to set an example: 'I am going to donate $1', 'I usually give to this cause yearly', 'I'll match your donation'.

instructions.context: Charity persuasion chat: the persuader tries to get the persuadee to donate to Save the Children.
instructions.question: What is the main dialogue act or persuasion strategy of the 'Persuader message to tag'?
notes: Classify only the message to tag; earlier turns are context.
Facts about the charity are credibility-appeal, facts about children's suffering are emotion-appeal, arguments that donating helps are logical-appeal.

criteria.greeting: Says hello or exchanges how-are-you pleasantries at the start of the chat. Includes the persuader's reply to a how-are-you question: 'Very well thanks.', 'I am doing well, thank you.', 'Doing alright..'.
criteria.closing: Says goodbye or wishes the persuadee a good day/night as the chat ends.
criteria.praise-user: Pays the persuadee a personal compliment, calling them kind, good, awesome or the kind of person who makes the world better. Includes praising 'you' for being willing to give ('it is wonderful that you are willing to donate!'); a bare 'That's awesome!' is acknowledgement instead.
criteria.acknowledgement: A short stock response that registers the persuadee's last message (agreeing, understanding, being pleased), with nothing new added: 'Absolutely', 'I agree', 'I understand', 'Great!', 'That's great to hear', 'Me too'.
criteria.filler: A content-free filler token such as 'Ok...', 'Fine...', 'yeah..', 'Indeed.', a bare 'Yes.'.
criteria.comment-on-partner: A reply that comments on what the persuadee said with the persuader's own view or a short answer, not a stock acknowledgement: 'That's a good idea actually...', 'We could all do better, I suppose', 'I do..', 'Yes, they are.'.
criteria.answer-about-self: Answers a question the persuadee asked about the persuader (their habits, knowledge, involvement): 'No, I don't donate', 'Yes, I'm familiar with them'. Replies to 'how are you?' are greeting instead.
criteria.confirm-amount: Repeats back or double-checks the donation amount the persuadee chose.
criteria.misc-other: Leftover talk: other charities, arguing or insulting, comments about the HIT/survey/task or about this conversation, asking for more, non-English text, typo corrections. Also neutral clarifying questions ('Which would you prefer?') and fragments ('Just think.').
criteria.off-task: Small talk with no link to the charity or donating: places, weather, hobbies, jobs.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks if the persuadee knows of or has heard about Save the Children.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's views, experience or habits regarding charity and donating, or whether they care about the cause (including 'Did you know <fact>?' questions).
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's own life: children, home town, family, life story.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Asks or urges the persuadee to donate or help, with no amount named, including 'if you could help these children, would you?'.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks the persuadee how much they will donate.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Pushes a small or minimal donation: 'every little bit helps', 'even 50 cents', 'any amount is welcome'.
criteria.donation-information: Explains the mechanics of donating in this task: taken from the task payment, $0 to $2, the research team forwards it, can be done now. Also practical details of other ways to give or help: no maximum when giving outside the task, tax deductions, payment methods, volunteering options. (Just pointing to the charity website to learn more is credibility-appeal.)
criteria.credibility-appeal: Presents Save the Children as capable and trustworthy: what it does, its programs, history, founder, reach, ratings, how funds are used, website, and answers to questions about the charity.
criteria.emotion-appeal: Plays on the persuadee's feelings about the children: suffering statistics, vivid images of hunger, war or death, 'imagine your own child', stories of individual children, expressions of sadness.
criteria.logical-appeal: Gives reasons why donating is sensible or right: donations make a difference, the charity depends on donors, the cost is small compared to the benefit, moral arguments like 'every child deserves a chance'.
criteria.personal-story: Recounts the persuader's own first-hand experience or something they witnessed, to support the cause.
criteria.self-modeling: Persuader says they themselves are donating, will donate or regularly give, as an example to follow.
